description: Curated verification dataset: famous English viewpoints (expected_high=true) and adversarial negative controls (expected_high=false). Researched 2026-08-23 with per-point coordinate arbitration (DoBIH v18.3, OSM nodes, Wikipedia geohack, Historic England).

viewpoints.name: Coombe Hill Monument
viewpoints.why_famous: The archetype site: Boer War monument on the Chiltern scarp with open grass foreground, steep drop and a huge panorama over the Vale of Aylesbury; National Trust flagship viewpoint near Chequers.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM way 605670840 (Coombe Hill Monument) centroid + peak node 11916869218 (260 m); Wikipedia geohack 51.75257,-0.77149 agrees within 50 m
viewpoints.notes: Monument stands right on the scarp edge; viewpoint and monument are the same spot.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] View from the summit over the Vale of Aylesbury: patchwork fields, a village below, long hazy sightlines to the horizon over a scrubby treetop foreground. Confirms the archetype exactly — this is the reference escarpment-edge panorama.

viewpoints.name: Ivinghoe Beacon
viewpoints.why_famous: Iconic bare chalk summit at the end of The Ridgeway national trail; near-360 panorama over the Vale of Aylesbury and Dunstable Downs; National Trust Ashridge Estate.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 31924506 (233 m) + trig survey_point 4018188064 + viewpoint node 1679011426, all within 20 m; Wikipedia 51.841985,-0.605755 within ~170 m
viewpoints.notes: Summit trig and viewpoint coincide; open in nearly all directions, steepest drop N/NW.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] Downward view from the grassy beacon slope over a large green field, a road, and hedged farmland stretching to a hazy plain. Elevated, open, long sightlines — archetype confirmed, though this particular frame is dominated by one big plain field rather than a rich patchwork.

viewpoints.name: Dunstable Downs
viewpoints.why_famous: Highest point in Bedfordshire; famous kite-flying and gliding scarp with sweeping westward view over the Vale of Aylesbury; NT Chilterns Gateway Centre and windcatcher.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 6443799173 (243 m); Wikipedia geohack identical (51.864243,-0.536344)
viewpoints.notes: Coordinate is the open crest above the London Gliding Club; visitor-centre lawn viewpoint ~450 m N at 51.8680,-0.5405.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] Mostly parched summer grass with a person in a camping chair, but the upper part shows the drop-off and a wide spread of harvested fields and hedgerows below — an elevated open viewpoint over the vale, confirming the archetype even if this photo undersells it.

viewpoints.name: Uffington White Horse Hill
viewpoints.why_famous: Summit of the downs above the Bronze Age White Horse chalk figure and Uffington Castle hillfort; celebrated view over the Vale of White Horse; highest point in Oxfordshire.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 249836029 (262 m) + trig survey_point 11212745463 at same spot; Wikipedia 51.5775,-1.56667 agrees
viewpoints.notes: Trig on Uffington Castle rampart; The Manger and Dragon Hill (51.57987,-1.56753) in the foreground of the N view.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Looking down across the chalk White Horse figure and the steep scarp into the Vale of White Horse, a green patchwork running to the horizon. Strong archetype match with the bonus of the hill figure; flat overcast light in this shot, but the place is clearly dramatic.

viewpoints.name: Combe Gibbet (Gallows Down / Inkpen Hill)
viewpoints.why_famous: 17th-century gibbet on a Neolithic long barrow atop a dramatic chalk scarp; classic hang-gliding site with a vast view north over the Kennet valley; adjacent Walbury Hill (297 m) is England's highest chalk hill.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM memorial node 3731509237 + peak 'Gallows Down' 9063870431 (280 m); verified against Historic England precise grid SU 36474 62235 -> 51.35802,-1.47756 (12 m agreement). Wikipedia coord is only a rounded gridref
viewpoints.notes: Walbury Hill trig (297 m) 900 m SE at 51.35246,-1.46505 (OSM peak 8088274; Wikipedia agrees).
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Grass-and-sheep foreground dropping steeply to a wide quilt of green fields, hedgerows and woods rolling to distant downs. Classic escarpment-edge panorama — archetype confirmed.

viewpoints.name: Beacon Hill, Burghclere
viewpoints.why_famous: Distinctive hillfort-crowned chalk hill overlooking Highclere Castle (Downton Abbey); grave of the 5th Earl of Carnarvon on the summit; panoramic views over NW Hampshire.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 1422934163 (261 m) + viewpoint node 348008239 at same point; Wikipedia 51.31278,-1.34361 agrees
viewpoints.notes: Steep open slopes on all sides; hillfort rampart rim is the viewing area.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] View from the summit fence line over wooded slopes toward a distant plain (Highclere Castle a speck mid-frame). Elevated and open with long sightlines, but the near ground is heavily wooded rather than an open steep drop, so the panorama reads softer than the Coombe Hill archetype.

viewpoints.name: Westbury White Horse viewpoint (Bratton Camp)
viewpoints.region: West Wiltshire Downs (edge of Salisbury Plain), Wiltshire
viewpoints.why_famous: Viewpoint at the top of Wiltshire's oldest white horse chalk figure, on the NW scarp of Salisbury Plain beside Bratton Camp hillfort; huge view over the Avon vale towards the Mendips and Cotswolds.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 1454304929 ('White Horse'); Wikipedia White Horse coord 51.26401,-2.14667 within ~180 m
viewpoints.notes: Westbury Hill top (230 m, OSM peak 6184881950) 500 m SE; viewing spot is the scarp lip above the horse.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Sweeping view from the chalk escarpment over a steep grassy combe onto a huge patchwork of arable and pasture fields fading to the horizon. Textbook archetype match.

viewpoints.name: Cleeve Hill (Cleeve Cloud escarpment)
viewpoints.why_famous: The Cotswolds' highest massif; the Cleeve Cloud crags on the common give the classic panorama over Cheltenham, the Severn Vale and the Malverns; on many 'best views in England' lists.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 345721292 beside peak 2414515700 (317 m) and trig 345777237
viewpoints.notes: Highest point of the Cotswolds (330 m trig, 51.91986,-2.00586) is 1.7 km SE on the flat common; the celebrated view spot is this escarpment edge.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] From the open common the ground falls away to the Severn Vale with Cheltenham below and the Malvern Hills on the horizon; grass foreground shows some tractor-rutted rough pasture. Elevated, open, layered depth — archetype confirmed.

viewpoints.name: Broadway Tower
viewpoints.why_famous: 1798 folly on the second-highest point of the Cotswolds; claimed 16-county view over the Vale of Evesham to the Malverns and Welsh mountains; one of England's most famous viewpoints.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 273120701 ('Broadway Tower', ele 312); Wikipedia geohack 52.02417,-1.83583 identical
viewpoints.notes: Broadway Hill summit (310 m peak node) 110 m S; open sheep pasture foreground with steep drop NW to Broadway village.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] An atmospheric misty shot looking down from the tower over grassy parkland slopes with walkers and bare trees — but the famous distant panorama is entirely lost in haze, so this particular photo does not confirm the wide-panorama archetype even though the elevation is evident.

viewpoints.name: Coaley Peak (Frocester Hill) toposcope
viewpoints.why_famous: Famous picnic-site viewpoint on the Cotswold edge with toposcope; sweeping view over the Severn estuary to the Forest of Dean and Welsh hills; Nympsfield long barrow behind.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 5969294880 ('Coaley Peak Toposcope'); peak node 434098760 (231 m) 200 m NE; Wikipedia 51.71095,-2.29955 within ~400 m (area centroid)
viewpoints.notes: Grass slope drops steeply W; a second OSM viewpoint node sits at 51.70943,-2.29926.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 5/5] Steep autumn-colored scarp slope plunging to an immense patchwork of the Severn Vale stretching to a hazy horizon — grass foreground, steep drop, vast layered panorama. One of the strongest archetype matches in the set and a genuinely stunning view.

viewpoints.name: Painswick Beacon
viewpoints.why_famous: Iron Age hillfort (Kimsbury) on an outlying Cotswold spur; panorama over Gloucester, the Severn Vale, May Hill and the Malverns.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM trig survey_point 1913396768 + viewpoint node 9908271072; matches DoBIH #17272 trig SO 86826 12100 (283 m)
viewpoints.notes: OSM peak node says 270 m but DoBIH height is 283 m - 283 used.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] View from the grassy beacon summit over the Severn Vale with Gloucester below and the Malvern-line hills on the horizon; open turf foreground and long layered sightlines confirm the archetype, though this particular shot is a hazy, muted vintage scan.

viewpoints.name: Leckhampton Hill (Devil's Chimney)
viewpoints.why_famous: Quarried scarp crowned by the Devil's Chimney rock pinnacle; classic view over Cheltenham to the Malverns; much-loved local landmark.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 1089669797 on the scarp crest; trig 1089670092 and peak (293 m) 250 m E; Wikipedia SSSI coord in same area
viewpoints.notes: Devil's Chimney itself stands just below the crest (~51.8639,-2.0790); the crest viewpoint used here.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 4/5] The Devil's Chimney limestone pinnacle is the subject, photographed from the escarpment edge, but behind it spreads a genuine wide panorama of Cheltenham and patchwork fields far below — the steep drop and long sightlines clearly confirm the archetype.

viewpoints.name: Dover's Hill
viewpoints.why_famous: Natural amphitheatre on the northern Cotswold scarp above Chipping Campden; home of the 'Cotswold Olimpicks' (since 1612); toposcope panorama over the Vale of Evesham.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 320946562 ('Dover's Hill') + peak 1579844369; Wikipedia 52.0551,-1.8022 identical
viewpoints.notes: OSM peak gives 225 m, NT/trig sources ~230 m; toposcope at the viewpoint.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] The toposcope pillar on the open grassy scarp top with the Vale of Evesham stretching hazily beyond; it confirms an elevated open viewpoint over lower country, but the dull winter light, muddy puddles and modest visible sweep make the pictured scene only moderately attractive.

viewpoints.name: Haresfield Beacon
viewpoints.why_famous: National Trust promontory hillfort on the Cotswold edge with an abrupt drop and horseshoe view over the Severn vale to the Forest of Dean; toposcope nearby at Shortwood.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak 326346334 (217 m) + trig survey_point 1913396767 (TP3627) + viewpoint node 1270255182, all within 25 m; Wikipedia 51.778022,-2.263028 within 90 m
viewpoints.notes: NT Shortwood topograph 1.8 km ESE at 51.77408,-2.25048 (OSM viewpoint 473800882) is the alternative famous spot.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Lush rolling green slopes falling away to the vale around Stroud/Gloucester with a wooded escarpment ridge in the distance — layered depth and a wide sweep over lower patchwork country that fits the archetype well, though no dramatic bare-edge drop is in frame.

viewpoints.name: Box Hill (Salomons Memorial viewpoint)
viewpoints.why_famous: Probably the most visited viewpoint in SE England: NT Salomons Memorial on the chalk scarp above the Mole Gap with a sweeping view over Dorking and the Weald to the South Downs; famed since Jane Austen's Emma and the 2012 Olympic road race.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint nodes 13810704 ('Box Hill Viewpoint', toposcope, direction 190) and 1326406797 ('Salomons') + trig 4267733568, all within 10 m; Wikipedia hill coord is the broader summit
viewpoints.notes: Viewing terrace at ~172 m on the scarp lip; open grass foreground, near-vertical drop to the Mole.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] The classic open grass slope below the viewpoint with picnickers, looking out over Dorking and the wooded Weald toward Leith Hill — an elevated open panorama over lower countryside that clearly confirms the archetype, shot here under flat overcast light.

viewpoints.name: Leith Hill Tower
viewpoints.why_famous: Highest point in SE England (294 m; tower top exceeds 1000 ft); NT gothic tower of 1765 with a legendary panorama - the Channel through the Shoreham Gap to the S, London skyline to the N.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM node 266529756 ('Leith Hill', ele 294) + viewpoint nodes 3689871823/12020056290 within 50 m; Wikipedia 51.17583,-0.36972 within 120 m
viewpoints.notes: Greensand, not chalk: wooded summit with open S face; widest view from tower platform.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] A hazy golden-hour telephoto view from the tower out across the Weald — misty layered fields receding to distant hills, confirming huge sightlines from the viewpoint, though the tower itself and any foreground are not shown.

viewpoints.name: Newlands Corner
viewpoints.why_famous: Celebrated beauty-spot on the Albury Downs above Guildford; open chalk grassland slope with a broad view south across the Weald to Chanctonbury Ring; famous as the site of Agatha Christie's 1926 disappearance.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 335941556 on the open slope below the car park; Wikipedia 51.233,-0.506 agrees
viewpoints.notes: Elevation approximate (~165-170 m at viewpoint); car park/visitor centre on the crest just N.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] Open grassy downland slope looking south over a largely wooded Weald with fields in the middle distance; it is an elevated open viewpoint over lower country, but the view is softer and more tree-filled than the dramatic scarp-and-patchwork archetype — pleasant rather than stunning.

viewpoints.name: Colley Hill (Inglis Memorial)
viewpoints.why_famous: NT open scarp west of Reigate Hill crowned by the 1909 Inglis Memorial drinking-fountain pavilion with zodiac mosaic ceiling and toposcope plaque; wide view over the Weald to the South Downs.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM way 237010049 ('Inglis Memorial') centroid + viewpoint node 12213730735 ('Plaque with directions and distances') at same point; Wikipedia Colley Hill 51.25639,-0.21861 is the broader hill
viewpoints.notes: Elevation approximate (~215-225 m); steep open grass slope directly below the memorial.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [other, beauty 2/5] The photo shows only the classical Inglis Memorial drinking-fountain pavilion against a wall of dense trees — a handsome structure, but no drop, no panorama and no open country visible, so it does not confirm the viewpoint archetype at all.

viewpoints.name: Gibbet Hill, Hindhead
viewpoints.why_famous: Second-highest point in Surrey, above the Devil's Punch Bowl; Celtic cross and trig on an open summit with views over the Punch Bowl and Weald to London on clear days; transformed since the A3 tunnel removed the road.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 251191 ('Gibbet Hill') + trig survey_point 776087291 + peak 262682, all within 10 m; Wikipedia 51.11611,-0.71611 within 80 m
viewpoints.notes: Main drop is NW into the Devil's Punch Bowl; widest open outlook N-E.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 3/5] The summit scene itself — Celtic cross, trig point, heather and bracken with a pine belt behind — with only a small sliver of hazy blue distance visible at the left edge; it shows an attractive open heathland top but does not itself confirm the wide panorama.

viewpoints.name: Wye Downs (Devil's Kneading Trough)
viewpoints.why_famous: The Kent Downs' signature viewpoint: dramatic dry chalk coombe (the Devil's Kneading Trough) biting into the scarp of the Wye NNR, with huge views over the Stour valley and Weald towards Romney Marsh and the Channel.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 1205697425 ('Millstone View Point') at the scarp edge; the Kneading Trough bowl itself is OSM way 104876151 centred 51.16830,0.97020
viewpoints.notes: Alternative celebrated spot: Wye Crown Millennium Stone 1.4 km N at 51.18134,0.96292 (OSM viewpoint 1212069369). Elevation approximate.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] View from the chalk scarp edge down a steep scrubby slope onto a bright patchwork of hedged green fields in the Stour valley running to distant downs — steep drop, long sightlines and vale patchwork that squarely confirm the archetype.

viewpoints.name: Devil's Dyke
viewpoints.why_famous: Britain's longest dry chalk valley beside a scarp-top viewpoint Constable called 'the grandest view in the world'; Victorian pleasure-ground history (funicular, cable car); NT site above the Weald.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 12895030267 (direction=320) at the scarp lip near the Devil's Dyke pub; Wikipedia 50.885,-0.205 (rounded) agrees
viewpoints.notes: Summit of the hill is 217 m; viewing spot ~200 m on the crest NW of the pub, drop to Fulking below.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 3/5] Shows the open grassy summit plateau with a viewpoint telescope, toposcope slabs and a memorial bench, with the low Weald just visible at the left edge. It confirms this is a designated elevated open viewpoint, but the photo is of the summit furniture (plus a parked caravan) rather than the panorama itself.

viewpoints.name: Ditchling Beacon
viewpoints.why_famous: Highest point in East Sussex on the scarp above the Weald; famous South Downs Way viewpoint and the notorious climb of the London-Brighton bike ride.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM node 33825466 ('Ditchling Beacon', ele 249); Wikipedia 50.902,-0.10694 agrees; trig at summit
viewpoints.notes: DoBIH height 248 m; sheer open scarp drops N to Westmeston.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Classic escarpment-edge view from the beacon: rough grass foreground dropping steeply to a wide hazy patchwork of Weald fields and woods stretching to the horizon, with the chalk scarp curving away at right. Strongly confirms the Coombe Hill archetype.

viewpoints.name: Firle Beacon
viewpoints.why_famous: Prominent beacon summit on the eastern South Downs scarp; wide views over the Weald, Firle Place and the Ouse valley to Newhaven; popular paragliding and South Downs Way landmark.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM trig survey_point 1543246088 ('Firle Beacon', ele 218) + peak 9137750946 (217 m) at same point; Wikipedia 50.8333,0.1 (rounded) agrees
viewpoints.notes: Trig on round barrow at summit; steep N scarp, gentle dip slope S to the coast.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 3/5] The trig pillar on the smooth grassy summit dominates the frame, but behind it the hazy low Weald plain and the rolling scarp are clearly visible, confirming an elevated open viewpoint over lower country even though the panorama itself is secondary in this shot.

viewpoints.name: Butser Hill
viewpoints.why_famous: Highest hill of the South Downs and highpoint of the old South Downs Way; vast panorama from the Isle of Wight to the North Downs; NNR with dramatic dry coombes (Rake Bottom); Queen Elizabeth Country Park.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 29267161 (270 m) + trig survey_point 3211457754; Wikipedia 50.97767,-0.9815 agrees
viewpoints.notes: Broad domed summit; steepest drops NW into Rake Bottom, sea views S.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] View from the hillside over green rolling farmland and wooded hills under a heavy sky, but the foreground is dead scrub and bramble rather than open grass, and the sightlines are moderate rather than vast — a pleasant but not stunning confirmation of the archetype.

viewpoints.name: Chanctonbury Ring
viewpoints.why_famous: Legend-laden beech clump on an Iron Age hillfort crowning the scarp; one of Sussex's most recognisable landmarks with immense views over the Weald; beloved of Kipling and Belloc.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 29543228 (242 m); Wikipedia 50.89626,-0.38177 within 80 m; trig (241 m) 500 m W
viewpoints.notes: Commonly cited height 238 m (Chanctonbury Hill); OSM node says 242. View N from the rampart outside the trees.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] A fine escarpment view northward over a rich patchwork of Weald fields, hedgerows and woods with long layered sightlines to a distant blue ridge; only a wire fence interrupts the grass foreground. Confirms the archetype well.

viewpoints.name: Glastonbury Tor
viewpoints.why_famous: England's most mythologised hill: conical tor with St Michael's Tower rising alone from the Somerset Levels; complete 360-degree panorama to the Mendips, Quantocks and Bristol Channel; Arthurian/Avalon legend and NT site.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 608628358 (158 m) + viewpoint node 8210677560; Wikipedia 51.14444,-2.69861 identical
viewpoints.notes: Perfect isolated-hill archetype - low absolute height but ~120 m drop to dead-flat levels on all sides.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] View from the Tor slopes over Glastonbury's rooftops and the utterly flat Somerset Levels running to a hazy horizon — a genuinely dramatic drop and immense sightlines over patchwork lowland, confirming the isolated-hill archetype despite the flat milky light in this photo.

viewpoints.name: Crook Peak
viewpoints.why_famous: The Mendips' most distinctive peak - a rocky pyramidal summit visible from the M5, with sweeping views over the Somerset Levels, Brent Knoll, Bristol Channel and Quantocks.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 312021397; height 191 m per DoBIH/guides (OSM node wrongly says 186); Wikipedia SSSI coord 51.2952,-2.8814 nearby
viewpoints.notes: Rock outcrop summit; open steep slopes S and W; ridgeline E to Wavering Down (211 m trig).
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Rocky limestone summit in the foreground with a steep drop to the Somerset Levels' field patchwork and the distant Bristol Channel — exactly the archetype (rock foreground, wide panorama, layered depth), though the M5 motorway snakes prominently through the view and the day is grey.

viewpoints.name: Win Green
viewpoints.why_famous: Highest point of Cranborne Chase, crowned by a beech clump on a bowl barrow; NT toposcope panorama from the Quantocks to the Isle of Wight, over the Vale of Wardour and Blackmore Vale.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 477241085 (277 m) + viewpoint node 2177842858; Wikipedia 50.9856,-2.1081 identical
viewpoints.notes: Toposcope photo: geograph.org.uk/photo/7025358. Steep scarp drops N; near-complete panorama.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] A view out from under the summit beech clump, framed by dark tree trunks, over a vale of fields and a handsome steep chalk coombe with yellow rape beyond — confirms the elevated viewpoint over lower country, but this particular shot is half-blocked by silhouetted trees rather than an open panorama.

viewpoints.name: Wittenham Clumps (Round Hill)
viewpoints.why_famous: Twin beech-clump chalk knolls rising abruptly from the Thames flood plain opposite Dorchester; immortalised in Paul Nash's paintings; 'the best view in Oxfordshire' with the Thames, Didcot and the Chilterns spread below.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM peak node 312636131 ('Round Hill', 120 m); Castle Hill (110 m, hillfort) at 51.62838,-1.17935 per OSM/Wikipedia
viewpoints.notes: Low absolute height but isolated ~65 m drop to the Thames; classic viewpoint bench on Round Hill's N side.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Open grass slope falling away to a wide sunny panorama of the Thames valley — the river, water meadows, trees and villages spread across a green plain. Confirms the archetype, though the hill is modest and the drop gentle rather than steep.

viewpoints.name: Tennyson Down (Tennyson Monument)
viewpoints.why_famous: The Isle of Wight's celebrated high down where Tennyson walked daily; Celtic-cross monument on open chalk turf with panoramas along the island to the Needles, across the Solent and out to the Channel.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 889473969 ('Tennyson Monument') + node 2433344 (147 m); Wikipedia 50.66647,-1.5415 identical; grid SZ 3249 8532 matches monument record
viewpoints.notes: Semi-coastal: sheer chalk cliff on the S side, open down N; included as the Isle of Wight's canonical panoramic hill.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] From the close-cropped down-top turf the view sweeps over the west Wight's fields, Freshwater and its estuary, out to a Solent dotted with sails and the faint mainland — a wide elevated panorama over lower land and sea that confirms the archetype, though this frame is mostly sky with somewhat parched summer grass.

viewpoints.name: Worcestershire Beacon
viewpoints.why_famous: Highest point of the Malvern ridge rising abruptly from the Severn plain; toposcope claims views over ~15 counties, E across the patchwork Severn vale to the Cotswolds, W to the Black Mountains and Wales. A celebrated Victorian resort viewpoint with a summit topograph.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SO 76883 45237, rock between topograph and trig point)
viewpoints.notes: Summit trig + toposcope; open grass ridge with steep drops both sides.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [other, beauty 2/5] The photo is a nighttime shot of a bonfire with a silhouetted crowd (a beacon-lighting event), with no landscape visible at all. It tells us nothing about whether the summit offers the panoramic archetype.

viewpoints.name: British Camp (Herefordshire Beacon)
viewpoints.why_famous: Spectacular terraced Iron Age hillfort on the Malvern ridge; panorama over Herefordshire and the Severn vale. Strong Elgar association; short steep walk from the Wynds Point (A449) car park makes it one of the most-visited viewpoints in the Midlands.
viewpoints.notes: Coordinates are the hillfort summit (highest rampart platform).
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 4/5] Shows the hill itself from a distance: a bare, dramatically terraced Iron Age hillfort summit rising well clear of the wooded slopes below, which strongly implies an elevated open viewpoint with steep drops. Striking place, though the panorama from the top is not itself pictured.

viewpoints.name: The Wrekin
viewpoints.why_famous: Iconic isolated hill above the Shropshire plain ('all around the Wrekin'); summit toposcope reputedly commands 17 counties, from the Cheshire Plain to the Welsh mountains and Severn valley. One of the most-climbed hills in the Midlands.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SJ 62836 08203; summit area 110m NNE of trig)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] Summit trig point with an open gravel top and a hazy but real view dropping away to patchwork fields in the vale below, confirming an elevated open viewpoint; the misty grey conditions mute the panorama in this particular shot.

viewpoints.name: Pole Bank (Long Mynd)
viewpoints.why_famous: Summit of the Long Mynd moorland plateau with trig point and toposcope; panorama from the Stiperstones and Welsh hills W to the Stretton Hills, Wrekin and Cheshire Plain N. Reachable by a short walk from the Shropshire Hills' gliding-club road (The Burway).
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SO 41521 94444, trig point)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] Open moorland summit plateau with walkers at the toposcope and long sightlines to layered blue hills on the horizon under a big sky, confirming an elevated open panorama; the immediate foreground is a muddy, puddled plateau rather than a dramatic steep drop.

viewpoints.name: Manstone Rock (Stiperstones)
viewpoints.why_famous: Highest quartzite tor on the jagged Stiperstones ridge (trig on the rock itself); wild 360-degree panorama over the Shropshire/Welsh border country. Steeped in folklore (Devil's Chair adjacent) and celebrated in Mary Webb's and D.H. Lawrence-era writing.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SO 36755 98648, rock 1m from trig point)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Taken on the ridge itself: a dramatic jagged quartzite tor in the foreground, heather moorland running to further tors, and the lowland plain visible far below on the left horizon — confirms an elevated, open, rocky ridge viewpoint with long sightlines.

viewpoints.name: Lyth Hill
viewpoints.why_famous: Shrewsbury's classic local viewpoint: a low ridge with an abrupt open south face giving a famous sweep across the Shropshire Hills — Long Mynd, Stretton Hills, Caer Caradoc, Stiperstones and the Wrekin. Home of novelist Mary Webb; country park with viewpoint benches and toposcope.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SJ 47198 06856, at country-park car park entrance on the ridge top)
viewpoints.notes: Viewpoint benches/toposcope lie within ~150m SW along the open ridge edge from this highest point.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 3/5] View from a grassy hillside over bright rapeseed and patchwork farmland stretching to a hazy plain — a genuine elevated open outlook, though the drop is modest and houses and a lane sit in the mid-ground; pleasant rather than dramatic.

viewpoints.name: Mam Tor
viewpoints.why_famous: The 'Shivering Mountain' at the head of the Great Ridge; probably the most-photographed viewpoint in the Peak District — sunrise panoramas E along the ridge to Back Tor/Lose Hill, N over Edale to Kinder Scout, S over the Hope Valley, with the huge landslip face dropping away E. Paved NT path from Mam Nick car park.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SK 12768 83615, by trig point)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [other, beauty 2/5] A roadside shot from the foot of Mam Nick: tarmac, a dry-stone wall, and grassy lower slopes, with no panorama or summit view pictured. It does not confirm the archetype (Mam Tor's famous view is simply not in this frame).

viewpoints.name: Curbar Edge
viewpoints.why_famous: Classic gritstone escarpment above the Derwent valley; sheer edge with boulder foreground and a wide panorama W/SW over Curbar, Calver and the Chatsworth countryside. Favourite sunset spot for photographers; minutes from the Curbar Gap NT car park.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM node 6645844485 (named 'Curbar Edge', on the edge crest); cliff mapped as OSM ways 42387693/377548428
viewpoints.notes: Elevation from Copernicus DEM (edge crest ~325-350m).
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Winter view from the gritstone edge itself: snow-dusted boulders in the foreground dropping away to walled fields, woods and the Derwent valley with layered hills beyond — a clear match for the elevated-edge wide-panorama archetype.

viewpoints.name: Surprise View (Hathersage)
viewpoints.why_famous: Named for the sudden 'surprise' reveal of the Hope Valley as the A6187 crests the moor edge from Sheffield; the rocky brow by Over Owler Tor gives a celebrated panorama NW up the valley to Mam Tor, Win Hill and Kinder. Popular pay car park directly below.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 1526099120 (plus Surprise View car park relation 4102748)
viewpoints.notes: Elevation from Copernicus DEM.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [other, beauty 3/5] Shows the famous abandoned millstones lying in bracken within enclosed birch woodland below the edge — atmospheric, but no elevated viewpoint or panorama is pictured, so it does not confirm the archetype.

viewpoints.name: Bamford Edge (Great Tor)
viewpoints.why_famous: Gritstone edge high above Ladybower Reservoir; the jutting ledges at Great Tor give the famous Instagram view over the Ladybower dam, Derwent arm and Win Hill. One of the most-photographed 'big drop' viewpoints in England.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 9936414082 ('Great Tor'); edge mapped as OSM cliff ways 26774595/377915793
viewpoints.notes: DEM reads 384m at the node; the celebrated overhanging ledge is on this tor. Photo shows the edge from across Ladybower.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [other, beauty 3/5] The photo is of the Ladybower Reservoir bellmouth overflow ('plughole') and dam, taken from water level; a gritstone-topped moorland edge appears only as a distant skyline. Interesting scene, but it shows neither the view from Bamford Edge nor the edge in any confirming detail.

viewpoints.name: Stanage Edge (High Neb)
viewpoints.why_famous: Highest point (trig) of the ~6 km Stanage Edge, England's most famous gritstone escarpment — climbing mecca and film location (Keira Knightley's cliff scene in Pride & Prejudice 2005 was shot on Stanage). Sweeping views SW/W over the Hope Valley, Bamford Moor and the Dark Peak.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SK 22782 85368, outcrop 40m WNW of trig point)
viewpoints.notes: The popular southern end above Hook's Car (~53.3465,-1.6290) is an equally famous photo spot.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 2/5] Shows the gritstone escarpment as a distant crag line on the skyline, seen from a muddy valley track below with rough grass and puddles in the foreground. The edge visibly is an elevated crag above lower moorland, so the place fits the archetype, but this particular photo is a dreary wet-day approach shot, not the panorama from the top.

viewpoints.name: The Roaches
viewpoints.why_famous: Dramatic gritstone ridge above Tittesworth Reservoir with Hen Cloud and Ramshaw Rocks; panorama SW over the Cheshire Plain reputedly to Snowdonia on clear days. Famous for climbing, Doxey Pool legends and the escaped wallabies story.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SK 00107 63892, benchmarked rock at summit)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] A wide open panorama from an elevated buttercup meadow over a green vale with patchwork fields and layered hills (Hen Cloud/Roaches skyline) in the middle distance. Confirms the archetype well: elevated, open, long sightlines over lower countryside, attractive flower-meadow foreground, though no steep rocky drop is visible in frame.

viewpoints.name: Stormy Point (Alderley Edge)
viewpoints.why_famous: Bare rocky platform on the wooded sandstone escarpment of Alderley Edge with a sudden open panorama NE over the Cheshire Plain to Kinder Scout and the Pennines. Made legendary by Alan Garner's 'The Weirdstone of Brisingamen' and the Wizard of the Edge folklore.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 539753711
viewpoints.notes: Elevation from Copernicus DEM.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 2/5] Shows a mossy sandstone outcrop overhanging a footpath, fully enclosed by woodland — no panorama or open drop at all. A pleasant wooded crag, but this photo does not confirm the open-panorama archetype.

viewpoints.name: Pendle Hill
viewpoints.why_famous: Isolated whaleback dominating the Ribble Valley; steep 'Big End' drops E over Barley. Summit where George Fox's 1652 vision founded the Quaker movement; inseparable from the 1612 Pendle witches story. Views to the Yorkshire Dales three peaks, Bowland fells and the sea.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SD 80465 41414, trig point)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 2/5] A stony track climbing a featureless rounded moorland dome toward the summit under a flat grey sky — nothing but grass and cloud, no view outward. The photo shows the summit approach, not the panorama, and does not confirm the archetype.

viewpoints.name: Rivington Pike
viewpoints.why_famous: 1733 tower on a gritstone knoll on Winter Hill's shoulder — Lancashire's best-loved short climb (Good Friday pilgrimage). Vast view W over the Lancashire plain to the Irish Sea, Blackpool Tower and (on clear days) the Isle of Man and Lake District; Manchester skyline to the SE.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 339320422 at the Pike tower; 363m is the OS spot height (DEM reads 349m)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 3/5] The tower-topped pike photographed from higher moorland (cotton-grass foreground), with a vast hazy Lancashire plain stretching behind it. It is a shot of the hill rather than the view from it, but it clearly shows the pike standing well above lowland with long sightlines — the place is evidently the kind of viewpoint we seek.

viewpoints.name: Sutton Bank (Finest View)
viewpoints.why_famous: James Herriot's 'finest view in England': the Hambleton Hills escarpment plunges to Gormire Lake with a huge patchwork panorama W over the Vales of York and Mowbray to the Pennines. Cleveland Way path along the rim from the National Park visitor centre; White Horse of Kilburn just south. The closest northern analogue to the Coombe Hill archetype.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 4605606647 on the Cleveland Way just S of Sutton Bank visitor centre; Roulston Scar cliff = OSM way 430247629
viewpoints.notes: DEM reads 279m at the rim (edge smoothing); bank top ~295m.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [other, beauty 2/5] Shows the A170 road cutting climbing the bank, with cars and a rock face beside the carriageway — a road scene, not the famous escarpment panorama. Does not confirm the archetype; a better photo from the cliff-top viewpoint is needed.

viewpoints.name: Roseberry Topping
viewpoints.why_famous: 'Yorkshire's Matterhorn' — the half-cone summit (cliff face from a 1912 mine collapse) gives a 360-degree panorama over the Cleveland plain, Teesside and the Moors. Captain Cook's boyhood hill; National Trust; one of the most distinctive summits in England.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (NZ 57903 12601, trig point)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 5/5] A striking shot of the distinctive half-cone summit with its craggy drop, zigzag paths, walkers at the trig point, and hazy lowland plain visible far below behind it. Photographed from elsewhere, but the hill unmistakably IS an isolated elevated viewpoint with steep drops over lower country — strongly confirms the archetype.

viewpoints.name: Malham Cove (cliff top)
viewpoints.why_famous: Top of the 80m curved limestone amphitheatre: stand on the famous limestone pavement (Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows camp scene) at the cliff lip with a big drop and a long view S down green-walled Malhamdale. On the Pennine Way; one of the most-visited natural landmarks in the North.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM cliff way 431606462 / attraction node 28887497 (cove); point set at cliff-top centre
viewpoints.notes: Inland limestone cliff top (not coastal). DEM ~300-314m on the pavement.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 4/5] An old black-and-white photo of the huge curved limestone amphitheatre seen from the valley floor, not the view from the cliff top. The sheer 70m wall makes clear the top is an elevated brink with a big drop and views down Malhamdale, so the place fits, but this image shows the cliff, not the panorama.

viewpoints.name: Tan Hill Inn
viewpoints.why_famous: Britain's highest inn (528m) alone on the moor at the head of Swaledale, on the Pennine Way — famous for its vast empty 360-degree moorland panorama over Stainmore and the northern Dales rather than a single drop. Named in the task brief; a celebrated high-point destination.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM way 315767859 (pub building); 528m is the well-attested signed elevation
viewpoints.notes: Broad moorland viewpoint, no steep foreground drop — weaker match to the escarpment archetype.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [other, beauty 2/5] A red tractor with a snowplough and a Union Jack on a gravel pull-off beside the moorland road — essentially a car-park/novelty shot. Open rolling moor is visible behind but there is no drop or panorama over lower country; does not confirm the archetype.

viewpoints.name: Castle Hill (Victoria Tower), Huddersfield
viewpoints.why_famous: Huddersfield's defining landmark: an Iron Age hillfort summit crowned by the 1899 Victoria Jubilee Tower, with a full panorama over the Colne and Holme valleys to the Pennine moors. Celebrated local viewpoint with road access almost to the top.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SE 15154 13989, ground by SW corner of tower)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 3/5] A dusk silhouette of Victoria Tower and a beacon brazier on the open hilltop, with distant lowland visible far below on the left horizon. Atmospheric and clearly an elevated open summit above surrounding country, but the darkness means the wide panorama itself is only hinted at, not shown.

viewpoints.name: Surprise View (Otley Chevin)
viewpoints.why_famous: The gritstone brow of the Chevin drops steeply to Otley with a celebrated 'surprise' panorama N across Wharfedale to Almscliffe Crag, Beamsley Beacon and the Dales — a famous Leeds-area viewpoint with its own Surprise View car park at the top.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 263010721 (Surprise View car park = OSM way 87832118; DoBIH The Chevin summit 53.893218,-1.69781)
viewpoints.notes: Elevation from Copernicus DEM (244m).
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] Taken from the Chevin's grassy edge looking down over Otley and Wharfedale: town, river valley, patchwork fields and distant moorland under a big sky, with autumn woods dropping away below. Confirms the elevated open escarpment-edge archetype well.

viewpoints.name: Garrowby Hill (A166 crest)
viewpoints.why_famous: The western scarp of the Yorkshire Wolds where the A166 plunges toward the Vale of York — immortalised in David Hockney's 1998 painting 'Garrowby Hill'. Huge patchwork-vale panorama W/NW toward York. Highest Wolds point (Bishop Wilton Wold, 248m) is 2km E.
viewpoints.coord_source: Estimated from OSM way 3084733 (A166) geometry + Copernicus DEM elevation profile; no marked viewpoint feature exists
viewpoints.notes: Point is on the upper bend of the bank (~185m) where the vale view opens; the exact celebrated spot is a stretch of road, not a single marker. Verify against the Geograph photo 'View from Garrowby Hill' (SE8056).
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 2/5] A dark, underexposed roadside shot dominated by the A166 tarmac and a red 'Dangerous Hill - Test Your Brakes' warning sign; the vast flat Vale of York is faintly visible stretching to the horizon beyond a scrubby verge. It hints at a huge escarpment-edge panorama but the pictured scene itself is a gloomy road crest, so the archetype is only weakly confirmed.

viewpoints.name: Orrest Head
viewpoints.why_famous: The viewpoint that converted Alfred Wainwright in 1930 ('our first ascent in Lakeland... its magic worked instantly'): a rocky knoll 20 minutes from Windermere station with stone seats and a full-length view SW over Windermere to the Coniston, Langdale and Scafell fells, S to Morecambe Bay.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SD 41424 99359, rock 1m NNE of stone seat)
viewpoints.notes: Fully accessible path since 2021 — a classic road-accessible short-walk viewpoint.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] From rocky/grassy summit ground the view sweeps over a beautiful pastoral vale of green fields, stone walls, farms and autumn woods to layered Lakeland fells in cloud. Windermere itself is not in frame, but this clearly confirms an elevated open summit with a wide panorama over lower country.

viewpoints.name: Latrigg
viewpoints.why_famous: Keswick's grassy balcony fell: an easy stroll (wheelchair-accessible route from Gale Road car park near the summit) to a bench viewpoint with the celebrated panorama S over Keswick and Derwentwater into the Jaws of Borrowdale, with Newlands and the north-western fells arrayed beyond.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (NY 27904 24715, inscribed stone at summit)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 2/5] Shows only a stony path climbing a bare grassy summit ridge under thick grey mist; no panorama is visible at all. The photo does not confirm the archetype, though the open summit terrain is consistent with a viewpoint on a clear day.

viewpoints.name: Surprise View (Derwentwater)
viewpoints.why_famous: National Trust road-side crag on the Watendlath road just above Ashness Bridge: a sudden airy drop with the classic postcard view NW over the whole of Derwentwater and its islands to Keswick, Skiddaw and Bassenthwaite Lake. One of the most reproduced views in the Lake District, steps from a car park.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 1277050135 ('Surprise View Point')
viewpoints.notes: Crag-top over wooded slope; elevation from Copernicus DEM (195m).
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 5/5] A stunning elevated view from the wooded crag high above Derwentwater: the whole lake with its islands, Keswick, and the Skiddaw massif under dramatic clouds. The steep drop and wide panorama over lower country are unmistakable — a top-tier viewpoint, though the foreground is treed crag rather than open grass.

viewpoints.name: Hartside Top
viewpoints.why_famous: Summit of the A686 over the North Pennines scarp (signed 1,904 ft) — repeatedly named one of Britain's great drives; site of England's highest cafe (burned down 2018) and a famous C2C cycling climb. Immense view W across the Eden Valley to the full Lake District skyline and the Solway Firth/Scotland.
viewpoints.coord_source: OSM viewpoint node 1381679200 ('Hartside Top') at the former cafe car park
viewpoints.notes: DEM reads 562m at the node; signed pass elevation 580m.
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [view-from, beauty 4/5] From behind a low stone wall at the summit car park, the moorland escarpment falls away to the A686 hairpins and an immense sunlit patchwork of the Eden Valley fields stretching to distant hills. The wall/car-park foreground is utilitarian, but the vast escarpment-edge panorama clearly confirms the archetype.

viewpoints.name: Winshield Crags
viewpoints.why_famous: Highest point on Hadrian's Wall (trig at 345m) on the Whin Sill escarpment near Steel Rigg — north-facing crags drop to the loughs with vast views over Northumberland National Park to the Cheviots and S to the Pennines; the celebrated Steel Rigg-Sycamore Gap stretch of wall runs just east.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (NY 74214 67561, outcrop 2m E of trig); Steel Rigg viewpoint = OSM node 999694418
viewpoints.notes: Short walk from Steel Rigg car park (OSM way 29485154).
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 3/5] Shows the trig point and Hadrian's Wall running along the open rocky crest, with hazy lower country visible to the north. Mostly a summit-itself shot in flat haze, but the open elevated crest with long sightlines over lower ground is evident, so the place plausibly fits the archetype even though the panorama is muted here.

viewpoints.name: Simonside
viewpoints.why_famous: Northumberland's iconic crag-rimmed sandstone ridge above Rothbury: a large summit cairn on the north-facing crags with a famous panorama over Coquetdale to the Cheviot Hills and E to the Northumberland coast. Rich in prehistoric remains and duergar (dwarf) folklore.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (NZ 02405 98710, large cairn)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 2/5] A gritstone outcrop on a heather slope photographed in thick fog with a white-out sky; no view over Coquetdale or anything else is visible. The photo shows the crag itself and does not confirm the panorama archetype.

viewpoints.name: Old John Tower, Bradgate Park
viewpoints.why_famous: The 1784 'beer mug' folly on the highest knoll of Bradgate Park — Leicestershire's best-known landmark. Open rocky hilltop with a 360-degree panorama over Charnwood Forest, the Soar valley and the city of Leicester; deer-park grassland foreground.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SK 52466 11134, rock outcrop by war memorial/tower); OSM viewpoint node 1110981901 nearby
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [hill-itself, beauty 3/5] Shows the castellated folly tower and craggy rock outcrops on an open grassy summit under blue sky, with a sliver of lower wooded country on the right horizon. It photographs the hilltop itself rather than the view, but the open elevated summit clearly is a viewpoint of the kind sought; charming scene, modest drama.

viewpoints.name: Beacon Hill, Leicestershire
viewpoints.why_famous: Second-highest point of Leicestershire, a country-park summit of ancient Precambrian rock outcrops with a toposcope; wide panorama over the Soar and Trent valleys — reputedly to Lincoln Cathedral and the Peak District on clear days. Bronze Age hilltop site and hugely popular local viewpoint.
viewpoints.coord_source: DoBIH v18.3 (SK 50982 14800, rock outcrop 50m ESE of trig point)
viewpoints.photo_verdict: [other, beauty 2/5] Shows a carved wooden statue of a shepherd with a sheep beside a drystone wall and autumn trees on flat grass — a park feature, not a viewpoint. No elevation or panorama is visible, so this photo does not confirm the archetype at all.

viewpoints.name: Haddington Hill summit (Wendover Woods)
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (a): highest point of the entire Chilterns (267 m) yet the summit stone sits in Forestry England woodland with, per multiple walk guides, 'a distinct lack of views' — 'the high point is surrounded by trees'. Tests failure mode: 'high but forested' — absolute altitude plus real escarpment prominence, but zero ground-level panorama. Adversarial pairing: it is 7 m HIGHER than the Coombe Hill archetype only ~6 km away, so any ranking driven by bare-earth DTM viewshed without canopy/landcover data will wrongly rank it above Coombe Hill.
viewpoints.coord_source: Wikipedia geocoding API (Haddington Hill); grid SP890091
viewpoints.notes: Summit marker stone 'Highest Point of the Chiltern Hills' east of Wendover Woods car park. Elevation verified 273 m on Copernicus DEM (canopy-inflated; official 267 m).

viewpoints.name: Blackdown trig point (Black Down summit)
viewpoints.region: Western Weald / South Downs National Park, West Sussex
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (a): highest point in West Sussex and in the whole South Downs National Park (280 m), but the OS trig pillar stands among pines and heather scrub with 'no major views, mostly trees' (trigpointing logs). Tests failure mode: 'high but forested' AND fine spatial discrimination — the genuinely famous viewpoint (Temple of the Winds, Tennyson's favourite) is only ~500 m south on the scarp edge. The algorithm must score the wooded summit low while scoring the nearby open ledge high.
viewpoints.coord_source: Wikipedia geocoding API (Blackdown, West Sussex); trigpointing.uk TP1443, grid SU919296
viewpoints.notes: National Trust land. Copernicus DEM reads 284 m (canopy-inflated).

viewpoints.name: St Leonard's Forest plateau (Barnsnap, near Colgate)
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (a): a local high point (~135 m) of the wooded Wealden ridge between Horsham and Colgate, entirely under mixed conifer/broadleaf canopy of St Leonard's Forest. Tests failure mode: 'locally highest but canopy-enclosed with gentle relief' — the hill has modest drops on all sides that a coarse DEM prominence measure may reward, but there is no open foreground and no panorama anywhere on the plateau.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed on wooded plateau; verified via Nominatim reverse geocode (Barnsnap, Colgate) + Open-Meteo elevation (135 m)
viewpoints.notes: Point is in forest ~700 m WNW of Colgate village; whole plateau is wooded so exact spot is not critical.

viewpoints.name: Haldon Forest high ridge (near Buller's Hill)
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (a): the ~250 m crest of the Haldon ridge between the Exe and Teign valleys, inside the dense Forestry England conifer plantation of Haldon Forest Park. Tests failure mode: 'huge theoretical viewshed, zero actual view' — a bare-earth DTM sees from here to Dartmoor, Exmoor and the sea, but the plantation blocks everything at ground level. Also tests discrimination from real nearby viewpoints on the same ridge (Haldon Belvedere tower, forest-edge clearings).
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed on highest DEM cell of ridge (Open-Meteo 250 m); Nominatim confirms Kenn parish, EX6 7XR (Haldon Forest Park); Wikipedia (Haldon Hills: highest points just over 250 m)
viewpoints.notes: Within ~1 km of Haldon Forest Park visitor centre; ridge crest is uniformly plantation.

viewpoints.name: Buck Fell plantation interior, Kielder Forest
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (a): a 337 m point on the flank of Buck Fell, deep inside Kielder Forest — England's largest man-made forest — several km from open ground in most directions. Tests failure mode: 'high but forested' at upland scale, plus remoteness bias — big elevation numbers and long bare-earth sightlines over the Border fells, but continuous sitka spruce canopy means no ground-level prospect at all. (Contrast with the open moorland tops like Sighty Crag or Deadwater Fell that poke above the plantation.)
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed in plantation SW of Kielder village; Nominatim resolves to Buck Fell, Kielder; Open-Meteo elevation 337 m
viewpoints.notes: Exact cell may fall in clearfell at some epochs (plantation is rotationally felled); the surrounding square km is forest.

viewpoints.name: Thetford Forest interior (Fire Road 12, Santon Downham)
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (a): local 'high ground' (~60 m — genuinely among the higher cells of Breckland) inside Britain's largest lowland pine forest. Tests two failure modes at once: 'high but forested' (relative to the very flat Breckland, this cell tops its surroundings, and a bare-earth DTM gives it an enormous flat viewshed) and 'flat with huge theoretical viewshed'. Nothing here offers any view but pine trunks and fire-road corridors.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Nominatim resolves to Fire Road 12, Santon Downham (inside plantation); Open-Meteo elevation 60 m
viewpoints.notes: Between High Lodge and Santon Downham. Whole plateau is plantation, so spot choice is robust.

viewpoints.name: Whittlesey Mere basin, Holme Fen
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (b): open arable fen in the drained Whittlesey Mere basin next to Holme Fen NNR — the lowest land surface in Great Britain (the Holme Posts, ~2 km SW, record ~2.75 m below sea level of peat shrinkage). Tests failure mode: 'flat with huge theoretical viewshed' — on a flat DEM a point here can 'see' tens of km in every direction with zero terrain occlusion, yet it is the opposite of a viewpoint: no elevation, no drop, no foreground, featureless horizon.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed on open arable (Open-Meteo -3 m); Nominatim: Seynory Drove, Holme; Wikipedia (Holme Fen) for context
viewpoints.notes: Deliberately placed on open farmland rather than in the birch woodland of the NNR so the control isolates flatness, not tree cover.

viewpoints.name: Padnal Fen near Prickwillow
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (b): black-soil arable fen at about 2 m below sea level, 2 km east of Prickwillow and ~6 km from Ely. Tests failure mode: 'flat with huge theoretical viewshed' plus the landmark-intervisibility trap — Ely Cathedral ('Ship of the Fens') is visible on the horizon from here, and an algorithm that rewards sightlines to famous objects must still not call this dead-flat field a viewpoint.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Nominatim: Lark Bank, Prickwillow; Open-Meteo elevation -2 m
viewpoints.notes: Nearest 'hill' of any consequence (Ely's clay island, 20 m) is 6 km away.

viewpoints.name: Tealham Moor, Somerset Levels
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (b): rhyne-drained grazing moor at ~2 m, interior of the Somerset Levels between Wedmore and Westhay. Tests failure mode: 'flat with huge theoretical viewshed' and landmark intervisibility — Glastonbury Tor, Brent Knoll and the Mendip scarp all stand on the horizon, so raw visibility metrics (many visible cells, famous targets in view) are high, but with zero relative height, no drop and a ditch-and-pollard foreground this must not score as a viewpoint.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Nominatim: Corner's Drove, Wedmore (Tealham Moor); Open-Meteo elevation 2 m
viewpoints.notes: The paired true positives are the surrounding hills that this point can see (Glastonbury Tor, Mendip edge).

viewpoints.name: Holbeach St Johns fen, South Holland
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (b): dead-flat large-field arable fenland at ~1 m near Holbeach St Johns, roughly 30-40 km from the nearest hill of any kind (Lincolnshire Wolds / Castor heights). Tests failure mode: 'flat with huge theoretical viewshed, far from any relief' — the purest flatland case in the set: no terrain occlusion, no terrain interest, enormous sky. Any positive score here is an unambiguous algorithm bug.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Nominatim: North Road, Gedney / Holbeach St Johns; Open-Meteo elevation 1 m

viewpoints.name: Romney Marsh at St Mary in the Marsh
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (b): reclaimed marsh pasture at ~2 m in the middle of Romney Marsh. Tests failure mode: 'flat with huge theoretical viewshed' in a coastal setting — the sea (a big open-water viewshed bonus in naive scoring) lies just beyond the shingle a few km SE, and the old cliff-line of the Kent hills rims the northern horizon, yet the point itself is an utterly flat sheep pasture with no prospect. Also probes coastal-proximity bias.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Nominatim: Chittenden's Lane, St Mary in the Marsh; Open-Meteo elevation 2 m

viewpoints.name: Vale of Aylesbury floor at Ellesborough (below Coombe Hill)
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (c): farmland on the vale floor at Ellesborough, ~1.6 km NW of and ~170 m below the Coombe Hill monument — this field IS the patchwork lowland that the archetype viewpoint looks at. Tests failure mode: 'in the celebrated scene, not viewing it' — the Chiltern scarp wall blocks the whole southeastern skyline, and the algorithm must produce a very large score gap between this point and its famous neighbour 1.6 km away.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed on vale floor NW of monument; Nominatim: Ellesborough parish; Open-Meteo elevation 90 m; Coombe Hill from Wikipedia (~260 m)
viewpoints.notes: The paired positive is the project archetype itself (Coombe Hill Monument).

viewpoints.name: Hope Valley floor below Mam Tor (Dirty Lane, Castleton)
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (c): fields at ~211 m on the Hope Valley floor west of Castleton, ~1.3 km E of and ~300 m below Mam Tor's summit (517 m, Wikipedia 53.34914,-1.81069). Tests failure mode: 'valley bottom directly beneath a famous viewpoint' — steep ground (Mam Tor face, the Great Ridge, Winnats/Treak Cliff) occludes most of the horizon; high horizon angles in nearly all directions should crush the score despite the dramatic scenery overhead.

viewpoints.name: Vale floor at Thirlby, below Sutton Bank
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (c): low ground near Thirlby/Gormire at ~146 m, directly beneath the Whitestone Cliff–Sutton Bank escarpment (~300 m at the top, ~1.6 km E), the spot James Herriot called 'the finest view in England'. Tests failure mode: 'valley bottom directly below a famous viewpoint' — the cliff walls off the whole eastern skyline while the open vale lies behind flat ground; the algorithm must separate this from the escarpment lip a mile away.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Nominatim: Carr Lane, Thirlby; Open-Meteo elevation 146 m; Gormire Lake ref coords from Wikipedia (54.24203,-1.22983)
viewpoints.main_view_direction: none (Whitestone Cliff walls the E skyline)
viewpoints.notes: Paired positive: Sutton Bank / Whitestone Cliff edge.

viewpoints.name: Severn vale at Guarlford, east of the Malverns
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (c): flat vale farmland at ~39 m near Guarlford, 3.3 km due E of and ~385 m below Worcestershire Beacon (425 m, Wikipedia 52.10464,-2.34014). Tests failure mode: 'sees a landmark but is not a viewpoint' — the whole Malvern ridge towers photogenically over this field and westward sightlines terminate on it, but the point itself is a flat lowland with a blocked western horizon and no drop; the score gap versus the Beacon must be near-maximal.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Open-Meteo elevation 39 m; Worcestershire Beacon coords from Wikipedia
viewpoints.notes: Paired positive: Worcestershire Beacon.

viewpoints.name: Chiltern dip-slope plateau near Dunsmore (Icknield Way Trail)
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (d): a point at 235 m on the enclosed dip-slope plateau near Dunsmore, only ~1.9 km SE of Coombe Hill and a mere ~25 m lower than it. Tests failure mode: 'absolute altitude without relative drop' — this is the sharpest paired control in the set: nearly identical elevation, same massif, same geology as the archetype, but sitting amid gently rolling fields, hedges and beech woods with no scarp edge and no prospect. Any altitude-weighted score without an edge/drop term will fail here.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Nominatim: Icknield Way Trail, Ellesborough/Little Hampden; Open-Meteo elevation 235 m
viewpoints.notes: Paired positive: Coombe Hill Monument, 1.9 km NW.

viewpoints.name: Kinder Scout summit plateau (highest point)
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (d): the actual highest point of Kinder Scout (~636 m) — the highest ground in the Peak District and Derbyshire — a famously featureless expanse of peat hags and groughs where the near horizon is the plateau itself in every direction. Tests failure mode: 'summit altitude without prospect on a flat-topped massif' — the celebrated views are all at the plateau EDGES (Kinder Downfall, Ringing Roger, Grindslow Knoll) 0.5-1.5 km away; the algorithm should rank the rim above the summit, not the reverse.
viewpoints.coord_source: Wikipedia geocoding API (Kinder Scout)
viewpoints.main_view_direction: none (flat peat plateau to every horizon)
viewpoints.notes: Open-Meteo gives 634 m at this cell; official 636 m.

viewpoints.name: Cranmere Pool, northern Dartmoor
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (d): the famous letterbox site in a shallow blanket-bog basin at ~550-560 m in the heart of the northern Dartmoor plateau, ringed by slightly higher ground (Hangingstone Hill, Whitehorse Hill, Great Links Tor, Yes Tor). Tests failure mode: 'high altitude with negative local prominence' — one of the highest test points in the whole set, yet a mid-basin bog with the skyline formed by nearby higher moor on almost every bearing. Altitude-driven scoring fails; horizon-angle analysis should catch it.
viewpoints.coord_source: Wikipedia geocoding API (Cranmere Pool); grid SX603858
viewpoints.notes: Open-Meteo reads 562 m at this cell.

viewpoints.name: Cotswold high wold plateau, Buckle Street near Snowshill
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (d): open arable high wold at ~259 m on Buckle Street south of Snowshill — full Cotswold-escarpment-top altitude, but set 2-3 km back from the scarp brink, where gentle plateau swells and drystone-walled fields close every long sightline. Tests failure mode: 'escarpment altitude without the edge' — the algorithm must fire on the scarp lip (paired positives: Broadway Tower 2.5 km NW, Dover's Hill, Fish Hill) and stay silent on plateau-interior cells of identical elevation.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Nominatim: Buckle Street, Snowshill; Open-Meteo elevation 259 m

viewpoints.name: Brindley Heath plateau, Cannock Chase interior
viewpoints.why_famous: NEGATIVE CONTROL (d): the interior of the Cannock Chase plateau at ~198 m near Brindley Heath — high for the Midlands plain around it, but a broad table of heath and conifer plantation where the surrounding ground is the same height or slightly higher (Chase top ~244 m at Castle Ring) and the relief is incised BELOW in valleys like Sherbrook. Tests failure mode: 'plateau interior with altitude but no prospect, partial conifer cover' — big regional prominence of the massif must not be inherited by its viewless middle.
viewpoints.coord_source: hand-placed; Nominatim: Brindley Heath Road, Brindley Heath, Cannock Chase; Open-Meteo elevation 198 m
viewpoints.notes: Mix of open heath and plantation; the control targets the enclosed plateau character rather than pure canopy.
